prompt: The gradient of a velocity–time graph and the area under it give, respectively:
options: acceleration and distance only if v is constant
markscheme: **B.** Gradient $=\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$ = acceleration; area = $v\times t$ summed = displacement.

concept: Acceleration as rate of change of velocity
prompt: A ball moving at $+5.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ is moving at $-3.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ two seconds later. What is its average acceleration?
markscheme: **A.** $a=\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{-3.0-5.0}{2.0}=-4.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Velocity is a vector, so the change in direction counts: the change is $8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, not $2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

prompt:
An athlete runs 1.5 laps of a circular 400 m track.

**(a)** State the distance travelled. **[1]**

**(b)** Calculate the magnitude of the displacement. **[2]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $600$ m **(A1)**

**(b)** After 1.5 laps the athlete is diametrically opposite the start **(M1)**: $r=\dfrac{400}{2\pi}=63.7$ m, displacement $=2r=127$ m **(A1)**

prompt: A ball is thrown vertically upwards, rises 5.0 m and is caught at the point of release. What are the distance travelled and the magnitude of the displacement?
markscheme: **C.** Distance is the total path length (5 up + 5 down = 10 m); displacement is the change in position, which is zero.

prompt:
A car travels 30 km at $60\ \text{km h}^{-1}$ and then a further 30 km at $30\ \text{km h}^{-1}$.

**(a)** Calculate the average speed for the whole journey. **[2]**

**(b)** Explain how the instantaneous speed at a given moment could be found from a distance–time graph. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** Times: $0.5$ h and $1.0$ h **(M1)**; average speed $=\dfrac{60\ \text{km}}{1.5\ \text{h}}=40\ \text{km h}^{-1}$ **(A1)**

**(b)** Draw the tangent to the curve at that time; its gradient is the instantaneous speed **(R1)**

**Common mistake:** averaging the two speeds ($45\ \text{km h}^{-1}$). The car spends longer at the lower speed.

prompt:
A ball is thrown vertically upwards at $15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from a point 2.0 m above the ground. Air resistance is negligible. Take $g=9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

**(a)** Calculate the maximum height of the ball above the ground. **[2]**

**(b)** Calculate the time taken for the ball to reach the ground. **[3]**
markscheme:
**(a)** At the top $v=0$: $s=\dfrac{u^{2}}{2g}=\dfrac{15^{2}}{2\times9.8}=11.5$ m **(M1)**; height above ground $=13.5$ m **(A1)**

**(b)** Taking up as positive, $s=-2.0$ m, $u=+15$, $a=-9.8$: $-2.0=15t-4.9t^{2}$ **(M1)**

$4.9t^{2}-15t-2.0=0\Rightarrow t=3.2$ s (rejecting the negative root) **(A1)(A1)**

**Common mistake:** using $s=+2.0$ m — the ball ends *below* its starting point.

prompt: Using a velocity–time graph for uniform acceleration from $u$ to $v$ in time $t$, show that $s=ut+\tfrac12at^{2}$.
markscheme:
The graph is a straight line; the area under it is the displacement **(M1)**

Area = rectangle $ut$ + triangle $\tfrac12t(v-u)$ **(A1)**

Since $v-u=at$: $s=ut+\tfrac12at^{2}$ **(A1)(AG)**

prompt:
A cart's velocity is $v=3t^{2}$ (SI units) for $0\le t\le2.0$ s, starting from rest.

**(a)** Explain why the equations of uniformly accelerated motion cannot be used to find its displacement. **[1]**

**(b)** Determine the displacement in the first 2.0 s. **[2]**

**(c)** Describe the shape of its velocity–time graph. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=6t$, which is not constant **(R1)**

**(b)** Displacement = area under the $v$–$t$ graph $=\displaystyle\int_0^{2}3t^{2}dt=t^{3}\Big|_0^{2}=8.0$ m **(M1)(A1)**

**(c)** A curve getting steeper (concave up) from the origin — the increasing gradient shows increasing acceleration **(A1)**

prompt:
A football is kicked from level ground at $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $35^{\circ}$ above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. Take $g=9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

**(a)** Calculate the horizontal and vertical components of the initial velocity. **[2]**

**(b)** Calculate the time of flight. **[2]**

**(c)** Calculate the range and the maximum height. **[2]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $u_x=20\cos35^{\circ}=16.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $u_y=20\sin35^{\circ}=11.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ **(A1)(A1)**

**(b)** Vertical motion: $0=u_yt-\tfrac12gt^{2}$ **(M1)** $\Rightarrow t=\dfrac{2u_y}{g}=2.3$ s **(A1)**

**(c)** Range $=u_xt=16.4\times2.34=38$ m **(A1)**; $h=\dfrac{u_y^{2}}{2g}=6.7$ m **(A1)**

The horizontal velocity is constant because no horizontal force acts; only the vertical component is changed by gravity.

prompt: A projectile is launched at $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $35^{\circ}$ to the horizontal (no air resistance). What is its speed at the highest point?
markscheme: **C.** At the top only the vertical component is zero; the horizontal component $20\cos35^{\circ}=16\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ is unchanged throughout. The acceleration there is still $g$ downwards.

concept: Effect of fluid resistance on projectiles
prompt: A ball is launched at an angle to the horizontal. Compare its motion with and without significant air resistance, considering **(a)** the maximum height and range, **(b)** the shape of the trajectory, **(c)** the acceleration during the flight, **(d)** the speed if the ball fell for a very long time.
markscheme:
**(a)** Both are reduced, because drag removes energy and opposes motion **(A1)**

**(b)** No longer a symmetric parabola: the descent is steeper than the ascent **(A1)**

**(c)** No longer constant $g$: drag adds to the downward acceleration on the way up, reduces it on the way down, and also gives a horizontal deceleration **(A1)**

**(d)** It would approach a terminal speed, when drag balances weight **(A1)**
